assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks combine a clean atomic-physics idea, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength where the light shift of the clock transition cancels, with a decisive experimental realization. They have pushed fractional uncertainty into the 1e-18 range, redefining what is measurable (gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale, searches for varying constants, a route to redefining the second). The impact is lasting and the discovery is clear and original. From the viewpoint of atomic many-body theory, the control of blackbody, hyperpolarizability and relativistic shifts is exactly the kind of quantitative atomic structure work that makes the claim solid.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice-clock concept and demonstrated early Sr clocks; Ye's JILA group brought the Sr lattice clock to the highest accuracy and stability and applied it widely. The two-person configuration fits the supplied credit well. Others (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, Hall and Hänsch on the comb side, Wineland on ion clocks) contributed nearby ideas and were partly recognised earlier, so the boundary of credit needs care, but the two names are a defensible core.
assessment.maturity: Mature: multiple independent groups worldwide (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, others) have reproduced and surpassed the original performance, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely, with the redefinition of the second under discussion and the field not yet saturated.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes could be read as incremental rather than a new discovery by some members.
Relative credit between the lattice proposal (Katori) and the long programme at JILA is a judgement call.
I cannot verify from the supplied text which independent groups first reached each accuracy milestone.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller's 1995 proposal for quantum computation with cold trapped ions gave the first physically concrete, experimentally realistic architecture for a quantum gate, and the programme built on it (experimental gates, entanglement of many ions, quantum simulation) established trapped ions as a leading platform for quantum information. The idea is original, clearly posed and has had a very large influence on AMO physics, linking to my own field's work with precisely controlled ions and atoms.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the theoretical originators; Blatt led the Innsbruck experiments that realised the controlled-NOT gate, deterministic teleportation and large-scale ion-string entanglement. Wineland and Monroe (the NIST and Maryland work on the first gate and the ion-qubit toolbox) are essential to the experimental story but are not in the supplied credited names, so the three-name configuration is a partial picture of the field. Because Zoller also appears in another candidate, any prize here would have to be judged against that overlap.
assessment.maturity: Mature: three decades of independent confirmation across many laboratories and platforms; commercial and academic ion-trap machines exist. Recognition is arguably overdue, though the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche) and the 2022 prize (entanglement experiments) cover neighbouring material, so novelty relative to those is the question.
uncertainties: The exclusion of Wineland and Monroe from the credited names makes the experimental credit incomplete.
Overlap with the 2012 and 2022 prizes may reduce the perceived distinctness.
Whether the prize should reward the proposal or the demonstrated quantum computing is unresolved; the field is still pre-fault-tolerant.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned cold-atom gases into controllable many-body Hamiltonian emulators: the observation of the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics, quantum gas microscopes resolving single atoms and site-resolved correlations. It opens the study of strongly correlated quantum matter with tuneable parameters and has changed how many-body physics is approached, which I find compelling as a theorist who values clean links between microscopic models and experiments.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical proposal (Jaksch and Zoller) and the first Mott transition (Greiner, Bloch, Hänsch) are central; Esslinger's work on fermions in lattices and the quantum gas microscopes (Greiner, Bloch, Kuhr, Gross) all matter. Four names are credited but only three can be chosen. I propose Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger as the experimental leaders and treat Zoller's theory as already counted under another candidate, which leaves the theoretical origin of the programme under-credited.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced: multiple groups across continents, with analog simulators compared directly against numerical methods. The 2001 BEC prize covers the underlying gas; this is a distinct step. Recognition would be timely, though the full impact on open problems such as high-Tc physics is not yet realised.
uncertainties: The decisive experimental credit is spread over several groups (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Gross, Kuhr, Hänsch), so a three-person split is contestable.
Zoller's theoretical role is not captured by my selection.
Whether quantum simulation has resolved an open scientific question, rather than demonstrating capability, is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed the mechanism of mass generation for the weak bosons, a milestone in the Standard Model and one of the largest experimental efforts in science. The scientific importance is not in doubt; the discovery was clear, and subsequent measurements of couplings have supported the interpretation.
assessment.attribution: The theory was recognised in 2013 (Englert and Higgs). For the experiments, credit is intrinsically collective across ATLAS and CMS with thousands of authors; the three credited names are founding spokespersons or conceptual leaders of the detector programmes, not individual discoverers. A prize in this configuration is possible but contentious because the Nobel statutes limit laureates to three and the work of the analysis teams is not captured.
assessment.maturity: Mature: two independent experiments saw the particle at 5 sigma, with a decade of follow-up measurements. Recognition is not premature; the question is attribution and the fact that the theory prize has already been given.
uncertainties: Attribution to three individuals is unresolved and may be viewed as unfair to the collaborations.
Whether the committee wants to honour the experimental discovery after the 2013 theory prize.
I do not independently verify the specific roles of the three named individuals within the collaborations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics brought the physics of an atom coupled to a cavity photon into superconducting circuits, reaching the strong-coupling regime and giving a scalable architecture for quantum measurement, control and readout of superconducting qubits. It is conceptually elegant and close to my own field of matter-light interaction, with the circuit playing the role of an artificial atom. It underpins today's superconducting quantum processors.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin, Wallraff, Schoelkopf and collaborators wrote the theory proposal and performed the first strong-coupling experiment in 2004. Four names are credited and only three can be selected; Blais's theory contribution is real, and I cannot judge from the supplied text exactly how to rank it against Girvin's. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is a close neighbour, which may affect timing.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature: reproduced across many laboratories and now the basis of commercial quantum computing efforts, though the quantum-computing outcome is still unfolding. The proximity to the 2025 prize makes a near-term award for the same platform less likely.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Unsettled choice among four credited names for three seats.
Whether the committee views the contribution as a discovery or an engineering architecture.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light reduce quantum noise below the vacuum limit in one quadrature and, through Caves's 1981 proposal and subsequent experiments, have become routine in gravitational-wave interferometers where they improve sensitivity to astrophysical sources. The concept is simple, original and practically consequential, and fits the quantum optics tradition in my field.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the key theoretical idea for interferometry; Kimble's group produced early experimental squeezing and cavity QED, and Schnabel's group developed techniques later adopted in the detectors. The first experimental observation of squeezing (Slusher and colleagues at Bell Labs) is not among the supplied names, and Mavalvala's role in implementation at LIGO is also real, so the attribution is incomplete and uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Mature: squeezing is installed in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, with many independent confirmations. Recognition is timely, but credit is diffuse and the gravitational-wave prize in 2017 already recognised the detector programme.
uncertainties: Missing the first experimental squeezing group among the names weakens the credit configuration.
Choice between Kimble, Schnabel and Mavalvala is difficult from the supplied text.
Possible overlap in perception with the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping and cooling of antiprotons, antihydrogen and positrons, with precision tests of CPT invariance and measurements of the antiproton and proton magnetic moments, form a clear experimental programme whose results (antihydrogen spectroscopy, antiproton charge-to-mass ratio, magnetic-moment comparison at parts per billion) test a fundamental symmetry. The experimental difficulty is remarkable, and the methods connect to precision atomic spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse (positron and antiproton trapping, ATRAP, electron g-2), Hangst (ALPHA, antihydrogen trapping and spectroscopy) and Ulmer (BASE, antiproton magnetic moment) are distinct leaders. Other major contributors (for example AEgIS and ASACUSA groups) might merit consideration, so the three-name set is not clearly complete. The relative weight among the three experimental strategies is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature: key results have been replicated within collaborations at CERN's Antiproton Decelerator, but no deviation from CPT has been found, so the case rests on technique and precision rather than a discovery of new physics.
uncertainties: No violation found; the prize case rests on method and precision.
Several collaborations share credit, and the three-name configuration may be incomplete.
The distinctness of the antihydrogen from the antiproton programmes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The thorium-229 isomer has an exceptionally low-energy nuclear transition that may be driven by lasers, with the prospect of a nuclear clock with unique sensitivity to variation of fundamental constants. Recent laser excitation of the isomer (2024) with direct frequency measurement links atomic and nuclear physics and is exciting from an atomic-structure perspective, since electronic environment effects are important.
assessment.attribution: Peik proposed the nuclear-clock concept; Schumm's group pursued doping in crystals and laser excitation; Ye's group did the frequency-comb measurement of the transition. Other groups (Tokyo, Vienna, Munich) contributed to the isomer energy determination and are not in the credited list, so the allocation is not settled.
assessment.maturity: Premature: the key demonstration is very recent, the nuclear clock itself has not been realised, and independent long-term confirmation and the scientific payoff are still ahead.
uncertainties: Not yet an operating nuclear clock.
Credit allocation among several groups is not settled.
Interpretation of the isomer energy and its environment effects is still developing; I cannot verify the latest results.
